issues.legal_issue: A longstanding court practice governing certified-copy preparation cannot itself operate as a rule of limitation barring an appeal.
material_facts: The appellant applied for a certified copy the day after the judgment but did not follow the local practice of notifying the copying department after the judgment was filed.
The appeal was dismissed as time-barred on the basis that the appellant was not entitled to exclude the entire period taken to obtain the certified copy, without an independent assessment of delay.
issues.conclusion: The local practice could guide the court’s exercise of discretion but could not be treated as a limitation rule; the delay had to be assessed independently.
issues.legal_principle: As stated in Chandra Bhushan v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, a rule of practice may indicate how a court should exercise discretion when considering laches or undue delay, but cannot be elevated into a rule of limitation that permits rejection without considering whether the party was actually guilty of delay.

predicates.appeal_from_limitation_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision dismissing an appeal as time-barred.
predicates.local_copy_practice_used_as_limitation_b: The court relied on a local practice concerning certified copies to deny the benefit of time spent obtaining a copy.
predicates.delay_not_independently_assessed: The court did not independently assess whether the party was actually guilty of laches or undue delay.

issues.definition: When an appeal is dismissed on the basis of a local certified-copy practice without an independent assessment of delay, that practice cannot itself bar the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: The appellant was not guilty of laches or undue delay in filing the appeal after obtaining the certified copy.
material_facts: The appellant conducted the litigation in person until filing the appeal.
The appellant applied for a certified copy the day after the judgment and obtained it after a prolonged period.
The appellant did not follow the local practice for notifying the copying department, and the High Court had not independently examined whether the resulting delay was undue.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not be said to be guilty of laches or undue delay; the dismissal was set aside and the appeal was remanded for disposal on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: A court must determine from the circumstances of the case whether a party was guilty of laches or undue delay; a practice concerning certified copies does not replace that assessment. The Court applied the principle in Chandra Bhushan v. Deputy Director of Consolidation and considered that knowledge of an unreported decision describing the practice could not readily be attributed to a litigant conducting the case in person.

rule.if: appeal_from_limitation_dismissal and appellant_litigated_in_person and copy_applied_for_promptly and copy_obtained_after_prolonged_delay

predicates.appeal_from_limitation_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision dismissing an appeal as time-barred.
predicates.appellant_litigated_in_person: The appellant conducted the litigation personally before filing the appeal.
predicates.copy_applied_for_promptly: The appellant applied for the judgment’s certified copy promptly after it was delivered.
predicates.copy_obtained_after_prolonged_delay: A prolonged period elapsed before the certified copy was obtained.

issues.definition: Where an appellant conducting litigation personally promptly seeks a certified copy but obtains it only after a prolonged delay, the delay is not undue and the appeal is remanded for decision on its merits.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a party lacks standing because the relevant premises have been derequisitioned cannot be accepted on the record when the asserted derequisition order is not produced.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the premises had been derequisitioned and that the appellant therefore lacked standing to prosecute the appeal.
Despite repeated opportunities, the respondent did not produce the asserted derequisition order.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not accept the standing objection on the available record, but gave the respondent liberty to satisfy the High Court that the premises had been derequisitioned.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to accept the factual contention without production of the order said to establish derequisition, while leaving the respondent at liberty to raise the matter before the High Court.

predicates.appeal_involving_standing_objection: The proceeding includes an objection that a party lacks standing because the relevant property has been derequisitioned.
predicates.derequisition_order_not_produced: The party asserting derequisition does not produce the order said to establish it.

issues.definition: When a standing objection depends on derequisition and the order said to establish derequisition is not produced, the objection is not accepted on that record but may be raised before the court hearing the matter on remand.
